Gastrointestinal Disorders

Gastrointestinal Procedures and Devices

GI procedures and devices in the ED are indication-and-complication problems: know when a tube or procedure helps, confirm where it is, and recognize the complications that need immediate consultation.

Board trap: A tube is not “done” when it enters the nose or stoma; position and complication checks are part of the procedure.

GASTROINTESTINAL PROCEDURES AND DEVICES

NASOGASTRIC ASPIRATION

Nasogastric aspiration is not routine for all GI bleeding. It is most useful when it will change management, such as severe hematemesis with concern for ongoing upper-GI source, small-bowel dilation, or selected toxin contexts. Many GI bleeds can be managed without NG aspiration.

ANOSCOPY

Anoscopy can identify anorectal sources of bleeding in patients with hematochezia, but only when technique is appropriate and perforation is not suspected. It complements the Ch85 anorectal exam rather than replacing inspection or digital assessment.

OROGASTRIC LAVAGE

Orogastric lavage removes pills/fragments from the stomach in selected patients presenting early after potentially lethal ingestion. It requires a large-bore tube, controlled airway when aspiration risk is high, and confirmation of gastric placement. Vomiting, aspiration, bronchial misplacement, pharyngeal injury, or perforation are the hazards that make lavage selective, not routine.

ESOPHAGEAL BALLOON (SENGSTAKEN-BLAKEMORE) TAMPONADE

Balloon tamponade is a rescue bridge for rapidly exsanguinating suspected variceal bleeding when definitive endoscopy or IR is not immediately available. Endotracheal intubation and suction reduce aspiration risk. Inflate the gastric balloon first, apply traction, and inflate the esophageal balloon only if needed. It buys time; it is not definitive therapy.

ABDOMINAL PARACENTESIS

Paracentesis removes ascitic fluid for diagnostic or therapeutic purposes. It is indicated for suspected peritonitis/SBP, diagnostic uncertainty, or symptomatic large ascites. Ultrasound helps identify fluid, bowel, vessels, and abdominal wall collaterals. Avoid scars, ostomy sites, and surgical areas.

For diagnostic paracentesis, collect appropriate fluid for analysis; for therapeutic paracentesis, monitor for hypotension, leakage, pain, and complications. Respiratory compromise or severe pain from massive ascites may be the reason to perform therapeutic paracentesis even in the ED.

TRANSABDOMINAL FEEDING TUBES

Gastrostomy, jejunostomy, and gastrojejunostomy tubes create predictable ED problems: leakage, occlusion, dislodgement, infection, peritonitis, aspiration, obstruction, bleeding, perforation, reflux, vomiting/diarrhea, electrolyte problems, GI bleeding, and buried bolster. Tube tract maturity changes what you are allowed to replace at the bedside.

TUBE REPLACEMENT

If a tube falls out, act promptly to prevent tract closure, but do not blindly replace immature tracts. Determine tube type, tract maturity, size, and whether a bolster prevents removal. After replacement, confirm placement with contrast imaging or other accepted local method before feeding. A Foley may be temporary for mature gastrostomy but should not be inflated in a jejunostomy tract.

OSTOMY COMPLICATIONS

Ostomy complications include obstruction, prolapse, ischemia, dermatitis, leakage, bleeding, appliance problems, and peristomal skin injury. Minor contact dermatitis may be managed with appliance adjustment and skin care, but ischemia, obstruction, significant bleeding, necrosis, or uncertain anatomy requires surgical consultation.
